source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Re-verified with the correct arXiv id. Majority voting over 5 first-round answers matches or beats multi-agent debate on average across 7 benchmarks for both models. Most of the debate gain is just ensembling.
numbers: N=5 agents, 7 benchmarks (Arithmetics, GSM8K, MMLU Pro.Med., MMLU Form.Log., HellaSwag, CommonsenseQA, HH-RLHF), max 512 tokens. Qwen2.5-7B avg: single 0.7205, decentralized MAD T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050, sparse T=2 0.7330, centralized T=2 0.6551, majority vote 0.7691. Llama3.1-8B avg: single 0.6203, best MAD (sparse T=2) 0.6990, majority vote 0.7242. Arithmetics Qwen: single 0.8140, MAD T=2 0.7600, vote 0.9900.
quote: Majority Voting accounts for most of the performance gains in MAD
limits: Small 7-8B models, one run per MAD cell, single-agent baseline averaged over 5 runs. Vote and debate share N but debate uses more tokens. Theory is a martingale argument; it assumes debate does not shift beliefs toward truth.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7: vote beats debate in this table. For one model, spend tokens on independent attempts plus a selector, not on attempts reading each other.

source: Chen (2026) When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
finding: Any policy whose output is one member model's answer (router, vote, cascade) cannot exceed 1 minus delta, where delta is the share of queries every model gets wrong. Average pairwise error correlation does not identify delta. On open-ended maths the all-wrong tail is about 2.5 times larger than a calibrated single-factor model predicts.
numbers: 67 models, 21 providers. MATH-500: delta=0.052 (17 of 330 fully covered queries), predicted 0.023 under full Gaussian copula; 90% CI for ratio 1.7 to 3.4, k=17. Code: delta=0.079.
quote: combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal
limits: Single preprint, one pool and one date. Claim is about checkable-answer tasks. Authors say they claim no new algorithm; the ceiling is classical.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable upper bound for any one-model attempt pool: the share of items where every attempt fails. Measure it on a dev set before adding diversity operators.

source: Chen (2026) Co-Failure Ceiling, Pillar B (matched-quality Self-MoA test)
finding: At matched accuracy, a low-correlation mix of different models beats Self-MoA (distinct samples of the one best model) by a small, real but partition-sensitive margin. Intra-model error correlation of the best model is very high.
numbers: Self-MoA rho_intra=0.80 vs heterogeneous rho_inter=0.42 on a 6-model accuracy-matched band (members 0.74 to 0.865). At k=3 equal distinct draws: mean gain +0.027 over 60 resamplings (range +0.010 to +0.050, positive in all 60); single partition +0.055 (CI +0.025 to +0.090). Higher-correlation MATH-500 regime (inter 0.59): +0.020, not significant. Slope of gain vs error correlation not significant under model-clustering (jackknife CI -0.07 to +0.34).
limits: Authors call the mechanism supported in one regime, not established. A mixed pool needs models of similar quality, which one-model agents do not have.
agent_relevance: Independent test of the Self-MoA vs MoA question (gap 8): mixing helps only at matched quality and gains are about 3 points. One model repeated has error correlation near 0.8, so attempt diversity from one model is weak.

source: Fadnavis, Kanakaraj, Wyss (2026) Beyond Consensus: Trace-Level Synthesis in Mixture of Agents
finding: Within one model (gpt-oss-120b), perturbed-prompt attempts and identical-prompt attempts have almost the same pairwise error correlation. Input diversity did not decorrelate errors.
numbers: Mean pairwise error correlation perturbation-diverse vs i.i.d.: 0.633 vs 0.603 (GPQA-Diamond, n=198); 0.571 vs 0.607 (LCB-Hard, n=171); 95% CIs overlap. Cross-perturbation answer agreement 82.0% (Fleiss kappa 0.681). Trace diversity (TF-IDF cosine) higher for beneficial flips: 0.585 vs 0.460 (p=0.015); dense embeddings p=0.0005, d=0.92.
quote: Error decorrelation is not the mechanism.
limits: One model, greedy decoding, preprint, authors promote their own method. Only surface-preserving perturbations tested, not meaning-changing ones.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: within one model, varied prompts do not lower error overlap (about 0.6 either way). Any gain must come from how attempts are combined, not from decorrelation.

source: Fadnavis et al. (2026) Beyond Consensus: perturbation content ablation
finding: Which kind of variation is used did not matter. Hand-written personas, paraphrases and model-written strategies gave the same accuracy.
numbers: GPQA-Diamond: personas 72.7%, SPUQ paraphrases 72.7%, GPT-generated strategies 70.2% (McNemar p>0.25). Controlled Polyjuice/Tailor perturbations 76.0% vs free-form SPUQ 74.0% (p=1.0). Stratified N=5 proposals beat 10 i.i.d. samples by +5.0 pp.
limits: Underpowered (n=198 to a few hundred); no-difference claims rest on non-significant tests. Same model family throughout.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 1: cheap surface variation is as good as designed approach variation. It does not test truly different algorithms (DIV-SE style), so the persona versus approach question stays partly open.

source: Fadnavis et al. (2026) Beyond Consensus: compute-equalised comparison
finding: At equal calls (7 to 11), one model with varied prompts plus an aggregator that reads all traces beat plain self-consistency and Self-MoA on most benchmarks. The aggregator reading minority traces is the active ingredient, not the vote.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b, N=5, k=2, 11 calls. BBH-3 (296): 86.5 vs SC 80.4 (+6.1). GPQA-Diamond: 73.2, +2.5 over SC, +3.5 over TextGrad; text says Self-MoA 64.1 (below zero-shot 66.7). AIME (90): 91.1 vs Self-MoA 90.0, SC 85.6. LCB-Hard: 62.6 vs SC 57.3 (greedy); under T=0.7 SC reaches 67.3. Minority-only traces 73.2% vs full traces 72.2%; answer-only inputs fall to the vote baseline. Full BBH: wins 91, loses 48 vs SC (65.5%). 7 of 12 pairwise McNemar tests p<0.05.
limits: The results table in the extracted text is garbled for the GPQA column; I used figures stated in prose. Single run, authors' own method, advantage on code is specific to the greedy protocol.
agent_relevance: Equal-call evidence for gaps 1 and 3: varied attempts plus a trace-reading synthesiser beat vote-only SC at the same call count, but an unanchored synthesis can collapse (Self-MoA below zero-shot on GPQA).

source: Yang et al. (2026) Understanding Agent Scaling in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems via Diversity
finding: Adding more identical agents saturates; varying models, prompts or tools keeps helping. Claim: 2 diverse agents match or exceed 16 homogeneous ones. A proxy K (effective channel count, from output embeddings) tracks this without labels.
numbers: Formal Logic (126 questions, so steps of 0.79 points). Table 7 vote, N=2 to 16 over Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B and a mix: heterogeneity gain from -0.80 to +11.9 points, mostly positive. Table 8: MIX beats best single model by up to +14.28 points at N=8. Closed models: gpt-5-mini homogeneous 0 to 6% vs 35 to 55% heterogeneous; gpt-4.1-mini debate accuracy falls 50.79 to 42.86 from N=2 to 16 even when heterogeneous. K embedding robustness: Spearman 0.91.
limits: Heterogeneous means models and prompts and tools together, so the effect of one-model prompt variety is not isolated. Near-zero homogeneous gpt-5-mini looks like a format artifact. Small benchmark counts, single runs.
agent_relevance: Supports diversity at small N, but the prompt-only part is confounded and strong models showed negative scaling. Gap 1 stays open for prompt-only variation.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Diversity Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Structural Coupling and Collective Failure in Open-Ended Idea Generation
finding: Group size gives shrinking returns in idea diversity. Interaction structure, not model weakness, drives collapse. Independent blind writing first (Nominal Group Technique) starts with the highest diversity; a subgroup topology keeps critique alive later.
numbers: Diversity utilisation ratio (Vendi score / N) falls from 1.03 to 0.47 as N goes 3 to 7. Embedding diversity metrics agree with human diversity judgments in 87% (Vendi), 82% and 81% of cases. 20 topics, temperature 0.7, 1,000 proposals per setting.
limits: Ideation, not accuracy tasks. Topology results are read from figures, with no table of tests. Preprint (an ACL Findings 2026 listing was seen in search).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports delaying sharing. An independent first pass then sharing keeps spread; dense sharing from the start contracts it. No equal-token accuracy test exists.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: Agents with partly different facts converge too early on the shared facts and never surface the unique ones. Failures persist across prompting, communication depth and group size and worsen as groups grow. A lightweight structured protocol helps.
numbers: HiddenBench: 65 tasks, 15 frontier LLMs. Multi-agent accuracy 30.1% under distributed information vs 80.7% for single agents given everything.
limits: Tests pooling of unique facts, not search over solutions. Only the abstract, intro and setup were read closely this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: early information sharing between attempts can bury minority evidence. A scaffold needs an explicit step that asks what others may know but have not said.

source: Shore, Bernstein, Lazer (2015) Facts and Figuring: An Experimental Investigation of Network Structure and Performance in Information and Solution Spaces
finding: In a human lab study, clustering (mutual awareness) made fact-searching less redundant but made solution-finding converge faster, including on wrong answers. Clustered networks performed better overall on this task; the ring did worst.
numbers: 417 individuals, 816 person-rounds analysed from 352 people, 51 runs, four 16-person networks (caveman, hierarchy, rewired caveman, ring). Clustering raised copying of neighbours' theories and convergence on incorrect answers.
quote: extensively share their raw information with their neighbors, but keep their working theories
limits: One puzzle task (information plus inference), student subjects. It also reports that Mason and Watts 2012 found inefficient clustered networks explored less, opposite to Lazer and Friedman 2007.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: share raw findings early, withhold working conclusions. Phase-wise sharing is a testable scaffold rule.

source: Lazer and Friedman (2007) The network structure of exploration and exploitation; Mason and Watts (2012) Collaborative learning in networks
finding: Second-hand through Shore et al. 2015 and a search summary. In the Lazer-Friedman agent model on a complex landscape, efficient (well-connected) networks win in the short run but lose in the long run, because less connected ones keep more varied solutions. Mason and Watts (human experiment) found the structural cause differed: clustered, inefficient networks explored less.
numbers: No figures read. Full text blocked (403) from three mirrors.
limits: Do not cite numbers. The sign of the clustering effect is contested between the two studies.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 direction only: speed from early sharing costs final quality on hard landscapes. Needs a direct LLM test at equal tokens.

source: Alexander, Himmelreich, Thompson (2015) Epistemic Landscapes, Optimal Search, and the Division of Cognitive Labor. Philosophy of Science 82(3):424-453
finding: Only the abstract page was read (full PDF blocked on philarchive, core and philsci). The authors argue that a strategy that deliberately seeks novel approaches (maverick) need not be optimal, that Weisberg and Muldoon showed no epistemic reason for division of cognitive labour, and they name errors behind that conclusion. They generalise the landscape model and say social learning should be doubted in epistemically complex environments.
quote: a search strategy that deliberately seeks novel research approaches need not be optimal
limits: Abstract only. A search summary adds, unverified, that Weisberg and Muldoon's model contained a programming error.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Weak evidence that an 'avoid explored ground' operator is not reliably useful; do not add it as a rule without a test on our tasks.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic Landscapes and the Division of Cognitive Labor. Philosophy of Science 76(2):225-252
finding: Search snippets only. Agent model on a landscape where patches are research approaches and height is significance; claims mavericks (who avoid ground already visited) help a population progress. Alexander et al. 2015 dispute this.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no usable number from the original; keep the maverick operator as untested.

source: Wallrich, Opara, Wesolowska, Barnoth, Yousefi (2024) The Relationship Between Team Diversity and Team Performance: Reconciling Promise and Reality Through a Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Registered Report. J Business and Psychology 39:1303-1354
finding: Average links between demographic, job-related and cognitive diversity and team performance are positive but tiny. Larger for complex tasks, creativity or innovation tasks and R&D teams. No sign of publication bias inflating results.
numbers: 615 reports, 646 samples, 2,638 effect sizes. All average |r|<.1. R&D teams r=.058 [.033,.083] vs .020 [.010,.029] others (p=.007). Creativity/innovation outcomes r=.056 [.025,.088] vs .020 [.011,.029] (p=.024). Firm-level financial outcomes r=.011 vs .033 for others (p=.012). Longevity and interdependence were not substantial moderators.
limits: Human teams, not search over attempts. Mostly correlational field data. Linear effects only; 33 of 534 English reports tested non-linear forms, and 58% of specified forms were inverted-U.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a realistic prior for diversity gain is small (r about .02 to .06), larger on creative and complex tasks. Expect a few points, not tens.

source: Earlier team-diversity meta-analyses as tabulated in Wallrich et al. (2024) Table 1: Horwitz and Horwitz 2007; Joshi and Roh 2009; Bell et al. 2011; van Dijk et al. 2012; Stahl et al. 2010
finding: Task-related or job-related diversity has small positive links to performance; demographic diversity has none or slightly negative. I read only the summary table, not the original papers.
numbers: Horwitz and Horwitz 2007: 35 studies, 78 effect sizes, task-related r=.10, bio-demographic n.s. Joshi and Roh 2009: 39 studies, 117 effects, task-oriented r=.04, relations-oriented r=-.03, overall r=-.01. Bell et al. 2011: 92 studies, 323 effects, job-related r=.05, demographic r=-.02. van Dijk et al. 2012: 146 studies, 612 effects, variety beta=.07, separation -.04. Stahl et al. 2010: cultural diversity with performance r=-.02, with creativity r=.16.
limits: Second-hand summary; original effect-size tables not opened. Definitions of diversity differ between papers. Study and effect counts were read from a flattened table and may be misaligned between rows.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: task-related diversity is the analogue of different approaches; its human effect is r about .04 to .10.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2026 v3) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: Resampling until a verifier passes is capped by the verifier's false positive rate. Weaker models have higher false positive rates, so no amount of resampling lets them match a stronger model. The optimal number of attempts is often below 10 once false positives have a cost.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (extended hidden tests as ground truth); false positive rate scales inversely with single-sample accuracy across Command, GPT-4o and Llama-3.1 families. At cost-benefit ratio 4 the optimal K is about 5 for all four models; at high ratios the optimal K is zero. False positive rate rises with K for Llama-3.1-70B but less so for Code Llama and Command.
limits: Code tasks with weak unit tests. Does not cover model-judge verifiers directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the selector is the bottleneck. More varied attempts only pay with a selector whose false positive rate is low (strong tests, not self-judgement).

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2026 v3) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Combining many weak verifiers with weights estimated by weak supervision selects far better answers from a pool of 100 samples than majority vote or a single reward model.
numbers: Llama 3.3 70B, K=100 samples, average over 5 reasoning datasets: first sample 68.4%, majority vote 72.2% (text: Weaver beats vote by 15.5 points), Weaver 87.7%, within 4.2 points of the Pass@100 oracle. Frontier references: GPT-4o 69.0%, o3-mini 86.7%. A distilled 400M cross-encoder keeps 98.7% of the Weaver gain.
limits: Needs labelled dev data or weak supervision across verifiers (judges and reward models up to 70B). The table layout is garbled in the extracted text; the majority-vote value is inferred from the stated 15.5 gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a good selector can be built from imperfect checks, but from several independent checkers, not one self-check.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own answers made results worse; a sound external verifier gave large gains, and just re-prompting with a sound verifier kept most of the benefit.
numbers: Summary table as read from flattened text (column mapping uncertain): Game of 24 standard prompting 5%, LLM critiques LLM 3%, LLM plus sound verifier 36% to 38%. Graph Colouring 16%, 2%, 38% and 37%.
limits: GPT-4 era, three toy domains. Column mapping of the table was read from flattened text, so use only the direction of the effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: self-verification by one model is not a good enough selector; use external checks (tests, solvers) where they exist.

source: Chen (2026) Co-Failure Ceiling: task format effect (abstract)
finding: The same questions give different headroom depending on answer format. In multiple choice the models rarely all fail; in free response the all-wrong tail reopens. So whether diversity can help depends on task format, not subject.
numbers: GPQA-Diamond re-asked in free-response: delta=0.127; five-judge LLM panel agreement rises from 0.73 to 0.92 (abstract). Pool-wide: tail underpriced 2.5x on open-ended maths.
limits: Abstract-level reading for the GPQA part; the mechanism (guessing on multiple choice masking shared failures) is my reading, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a proxy for landscape type is whether answers can be guessed or checked cheaply. Multiple-choice benchmarks may overstate diversity gains because chance-level answers hide shared failures.
